models.title: Fisher ideal bilateral price index
models.summary: Fisher combines the corresponding Laspeyres and Paasche indexes by their geometric mean.

relationship.locator: Learning Module4, Measuring Inflation: The Construction of Price Indexes, printed p250 (PDF p262), unnumbered Fisher formula
relationship.translation_notes: Both inputs are dimensionless base-one ratios. The square root preserves a dimensionless price index. V1 geometric-mean arithmetic is a dependency; this record defines the independently meaningful Fisher weighting construction rather than a renamed generic mean.

variables.context: Same security, currency, nominal/real basis, timing and period frequency as other quantities in this relationship

variables.definition: Nonnegative geometric mean of the two compatible bilateral price indexes
variables.context: Same security, currency, nominal/real basis, timing and period frequency as other quantities in this relationship

assumptions: Source assumption: both indexes concern the same periods, item coverage and normalization.
Source assumption: choose the nonnegative square-root branch.
limitations: The bilateral Fisher formula alone does not chain multiple periods; chaining requires a separate product of compatible adjacent index relatives.

models.title: Inflation from a consistent price-index series
models.summary: Inflation is the proportional change in the chosen aggregate price index between the stated periods.

relationship.locator: Learning Module4, Inflation / Measuring Inflation, printed pp246,249 (PDF pp258,261), unnumbered definition and Exhibit20 example
relationship.translation_notes: Dimensionless index ratio minus pure1 is a base fractional inflation rate. The same arithmetic as output growth has a different independently defined quantity: aggregate price change rather than real output change. No percent conversion factor is inserted.

limitations: A one-good relative price change does not by itself measure aggregate inflation.
Changing index reference units cancels in the ratio; rebasing only one observation does not.
